strengths: The paper addresses a clear gap in the model soups literature: extending soups to self-supervised ingredients, and is the first to show LMC can hold between ingredients trained with different SSL algorithms (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR), which is a genuinely novel empirical finding.

The experimental scope is broad: ImageNet with multiple shifted/robustness test sets (ImageNet-C, LAION-C, ImageNet-A/R/V2/ReaL/HR), 21-task VTAB transfer with a custom mini-VTAB-C corruption benchmark, and a second stock (Franca) to show generality.

The proposed 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline is a fair and well-matched control that isolates the specific contribution of mixing across differing SSL runs (not just having more/longer training), strengthening the causal claims.

The additional contributions (Self-Seasoning for label-free mixture selection, combination with test-time adaptation, demonstration on an alternate stock) show reasonable exploration of the idea's implications and robustness of the finding across settings.

The presentation with the soup/ingredient/stock analogy and diagrams (Figs. 1, 3) clearly communicates the relationship to prior work (Model Soups, Ratatouille) and precisely formalizes the method with an explicit equation.
Reasonably thorough implementation details are provided in the appendix (hyperparameter sweeps, optimizer settings, augmentation, SSL configurations), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The reported gains from Self-Souping (excluding the shift-aware inter-training experiment) are frequently very small (e.g., ~+1% on ImageNet-C, +0.4% on LAION-C, and often <1% on VTAB), and no statistical significance testing, variance across seeds, or confidence intervals are reported anywhere, making it hard to know whether these differences are meaningful versus noise from a single run per configuration.

The headline +3.5%/+7% robustness gains (§4.3) rely on inter-training directly on the (unlabeled) target corrupted distribution, which is a much stronger and less general setup than the other experiments; this is somewhat conflated in the abstract with the more modest 'algorithm diversity' gains, potentially overstating the generality of the core Self-Soupervision idea.

Only 3 SSL algorithms (one per family) and a limited/small-scale experimental regime (ViT-B, short inter-training schedules of 5-10 epochs or 10-100K steps, small subsets like mini-VTAB with 1K samples) are used; it is unclear whether findings generalize to longer training, larger models, or other SSL methods, and the paper's own limitations section concedes this without providing supporting ablations.

The comparison in Table 1/2 selects 'best ingredient' and 'greedy search' based on ImageNet-Val accuracy, which can make the reported metric not the best possible result for other test sets (acknowledged in text), complicating fair comparison across methods and potentially underselling or overselling different baselines inconsistently.

The Self-Seasoning results (Table 5, §4.5) are mixed at best: it is only the best method on 4/21 tasks and can substantially underperform supervised seasoning and even the best single ingredient on several structured tasks (e.g., Clevr-Count 17.5 vs 33.7, dSpr-Loc-X 4.1 vs 11.6), which somewhat undercuts the claim that Self-Seasoning is broadly 'competitive.'

The relationship to model merging/multi-task SSL/domain adaptation is discussed only qualitatively; no quantitative comparison against any of these alternative approaches (e.g., TIES-merging, joint multi-task SSL) is provided, leaving open whether the specific 'separate inter-train then average' recipe is actually preferable to these alternatives in practice.
Some data/code links in the appendix (§C) appear to be placeholders ('Data.' / 'Code.' with no actual content), raising concerns about reproducibility support at submission time.

strengths: The paper presents a natural and well-motivated generalization of model soups to the self-supervised setting, and is the first to empirically demonstrate that linear mode connectivity (LMC) can hold across ingredients trained with fundamentally different SSL losses (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR, LeJEPA), which is a genuinely novel empirical finding.

The experimental scope is broad: ImageNet and its many shifted test sets (ReaL, V2, HR, A, R, C), LAION-C, and 21 VTAB tasks with a custom mini-VTAB-C benchmark, giving reasonably comprehensive coverage of the claims.

The paper includes well-designed, fair baselines (e.g., 'continued SSL + supervised soup') that control for search/development cost, which strengthens the claim that gains come specifically from souping across differing SSL runs rather than merely from extra training.

The proposed Self-Seasoning method, which mixes purely self-supervised ingredients without any labels via kNN-entropy minimization, is a creative and practically useful contribution for low-label regimes, and is empirically shown to be competitive with labeled seasoning.

The paper provides substantial reproducibility detail (training hyperparameters, learning-rate sweeps, code snippet for Self-Seasoning, appendix ablations with alternate augmentations and an alternate stock), and an honest limitations section.

The demonstrated robustness gains under distribution shift (particularly inter-training on corrupted/test-like unlabeled data before fine-tuning) are the paper's most compelling and practically significant results (+3.5% IN-C, +7% LAION-C).
weaknesses: Many of the reported gains are quite small (often <1%) on the primary in-distribution benchmarks (ImageNet-Val, VTAB clean accuracy), and the practical significance of these modest gains versus added SSL inter-training compute is not fully quantified against increased training cost.

Results are largely reported as single-run numbers without confidence intervals, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing, making it hard to assess whether the (frequently small) differences between soup types are robust or within noise, especially given the fine granularity of some tables (e.g., differences of 0.1-0.3%).

The core methodological contribution is conceptually a fairly direct combination of existing ideas (Model Soups + Model Ratatouille's inter-training scheme, substituting SSL losses for supervised losses), so the technical novelty is more in the empirical demonstration than in new algorithmic machinery.

Generalization across architectures/stocks is only lightly tested (one additional Franca stock ablation with 2 SSL algorithms), leaving open how well the findings transfer beyond ViT-B/MAE-style initializations.

The few-shot Self-Seasoning results (Table 9, Fig. 4) show that its advantage over plain fine-tuning vanishes or reverses as N grows past a few hundred samples, especially on specialized/structured VTAB tasks, which somewhat narrows the claimed practical utility to a fairly specific low-data regime that is not strongly emphasized in the main text.

The mini-VTAB/mini-VTAB-C subsets (1K train/test) and the 15-corruption synthetic shift construction are custom benchmarks without external validation, which could affect the generality of the transfer/robustness conclusions in §4.4.

The paper's discussion of *why* LMC holds across differently-trained SSL ingredients is largely empirical/observational; there is no theoretical or mechanistic analysis explaining this surprising phenomenon, which is flagged as a novel finding but left unexplained.
